article.title: Descent Into Fascism
article.author: Sharon Kyle, Dick Price, Henry A. Giroux
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. What happens when cruelty becomes a governing philosophy? When political leaders celebrate violence, billionaires wield extraordinary influence over government, and institutions supposedly designed to defend democracy become instruments of repression? These questions were at the center of our recent conversation with political theorist Henry Giroux, whose latest LA Progressive essay, "The Politics of the Abyss: MAGA, Moral Rot, and the Struggle for the Future," examines what he considers the accelerating collapse of America's democratic and moral foundations. Giroux, who holds the McMaster University Chair for Scholarship in the Public Interest, offered an unsparing assessment of contemporary American politics. But our conversation went considerably beyond Donald Trump and MAGA. It explored how the United States arrived at this moment—and whether Americans can imagine and construct a different future. Henry Giroux: Descent into Fascism (30:56) The Collapse of Conscience Giroux began by discussing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his embrace of military power, violence, and the spectacle of punishment. For Giroux, the issue extends beyond individual incompetence or corruption. Hegseth represents a political culture that increasingly celebrates aggression, domination, and authoritarian masculinity. Giroux described the underlying problem as "the collapse of conscience." This moral deterioration, he argued, is reflected not only in the celebration of violence but in the treatment of entire populations as disposable. He distinguished between disposability , in which certain people are denied the resources necessary to live dignified lives, and disappearance , in which people are effectively erased from public recognition, legal protection, and historical memory. Immigration enforcement, attacks on due process, and the normalization of state violence exemplify this larger transformation. Related: The Politics of the Abyss: MAGA, Moral Rot, and the Struggle for the Future But Sharon raised a question that shifted our discussion from political leadership to the American public itself: What does it say about the population that these developments can occur so openly? Giroux's answer pointed toward the institutions that shape public consciousness. How Americans Learned to Accept Authoritarianism "People learn to be racist," Giroux observed. They also learn to embrace ignorance, distrust intellectuals, and accept domination. That learning doesn't occur in a vacuum. Schools, universities, television, social media, and other cultural institutions help shape what people consider normal, legitimate, or desirable. Giroux argued that decades of neoliberalism have encouraged Americans to understand themselves primarily as isolated individuals competing for personal advantage. Under this ideology, self-interest becomes the organizing principle of society, empathy becomes a liability, and solidarity is displaced by competition. "We live in a country that should be appropriately called gangster capitalism," he declared. And, in his formulation, gangster capitalism produces a population increasingly accustomed to its values. The Powell Memo and the Counterrevolution Against the 1960s One of the most revealing exchanges occurred when Sharon raised the 1971 Powell Memo, written by corporate attorney Lewis Powell shortly before his appointment to the Supreme Court. She situated the memorandum within a much longer American history of racial domination, arguing that the reaction against the civil rights, women's liberation, and antiwar movements represented an effort to restore forms of power those movements had begun to challenge. Giroux agreed but added an important distinction. "The Powell memo was the first shot in a counter-revolution," he said. Related: What I Learned Along the Way: Memory, Education,and the Struggle for the Future Its significance, he explained, was that corporate conservatives recognized that maintaining their power required more than government repression. They needed to control ideas. They needed think tanks, influence over universities, and institutions capable of shaping public understanding. The struggles of the 1960s had demonstrated that education could do more than prepare people for employment. It could encourage critical thinking, challenge hierarchy, expand democratic participation, and help previously excluded communities demand power. Conservative elites recognized that possibility as a threat. For Giroux, the subsequent decades witnessed the expansion of a coordinated cultural and political project that increasingly transformed education from a potential instrument of liberation into an instrument of conformity. Today, with artificial intelligence and powerful digital platforms, the reach of those institutions extends into nearly every corner of American life. Will Electing Democrats Be Enough? We asked Giroux whether the United States could experience the kind of fundamental transformation that seemed possible during the 1960s. After all, even if Democrats regain control of Congress or the presidency, wouldn't something much deeper have to change? Giroux was emphatic. "The Democrats may win Congress. But it doesn't mean much really if ... the Schumers of the Democratic Party control Congress," he argued. His criticism extended beyond electoral tactics to the party's relationship with capitalism, militarism, and concentrated wealth. He identified Bernie Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and younger political movements as signs that important changes may be underway. Related: From Monsters to Machinery: How Fascism Is Made Particularly encouraging, he said, is the growing willingness of young Americans to consider socialism and reject the anticommunist rhetoric that shaped earlier generations. The possibilities for transformation exist, he suggested, but they cannot be reduced to replacing one set of elected officials with another. Hope Requires Political Action Perhaps Giroux's most important observation concerned hope. Sharon noted that many Americans, particularly those historically excluded from meaningful democratic participation, never fully accepted the claim that the United States was a democracy in the first place. Giroux acknowledged that history but warned against abandoning hope altogether. "I don't see how agency can exist without hope and hope can exist without agency," he said. Without the capacity to imagine a different future, people risk accepting the existing political order as inevitable. He pointed to youth movements internationally as evidence that younger generations are beginning to challenge not merely individual policies but the political and economic arrangements that produce inequality. For Giroux, democratic struggle requires more than outrage and resistance. It requires the imagination to envision something fundamentally different. Our conversation ended on a personal note. Giroux expressed his hope that he might someday return to the United States and participate in gatherings such as our recent Left Coast Forum. For now, he said, he is afraid to cross the border. That admission underscored the seriousness of his warnings. Related: Jason Arday and the Machinery of Racialized Disposability Yet his central message was not resignation. It was that education, political imagination, and collective struggle remain indispensable to the construction of a more democratic future. The question isn't simply whether Americans can defeat Trump. It's whether we can build a society that no longer produces the conditions that made Trumpism possible.
